title: A New Year’s Milestone
body:
Dear friend,

Happy New Year.

In Japan, decorations called kadomatsu stand at the entrances to homes and shops during the New Year season. They are a sign of celebration, welcoming the year ahead.

There is a New Year’s story told about Ikkyū, a Japanese monk of the Rinzai school of Zen Buddhism. As people celebrated, he is said to have walked through town carrying a staff with a skull on its tip, calling out, “Take care! Take care!”

Why bring a skull to a celebration? A poem traditionally attributed to Ikkyū offers a clue:

The New Year’s decorations are milestones
on the journey to the world beyond—
cause for celebration, and yet not.

Each new year means that we have grown another year older. The decorations mark that joy, but they also mark another step on our journey toward death. The poem holds both meanings together.

In the West, there is the Latin phrase memento mori: “Remember that you must die.” Skulls in paintings and other works of art remind us that our lives are finite. I hear something similar in the story of Ikkyū.

At the beginning of a new year, plans and wishes come naturally. This year, I want to do this. I want to spend time with someone I love. Yet we do not know how much time we have.

“Cause for celebration, and yet not.” I want to take both sides of this poem to heart. It is a joy to welcome a new year. At the same time, we will not live forever. Both are true.

Ikkyū’s “Take care!” is a startling call amid the festivities. When I recall it in the joy of the New Year, I notice how easily I have assumed that another year will simply be given to me. Here we are, alive now, welcoming the year with others. I feel grateful for that all over again.

May the new year be a good one for you.

Keeping the limits of our lives in mind, let us celebrate its beginning together.
